issues.subcategory: intervention timing contradiction
issues.description: The manuscript gives mutually contradictory accounts of when the resistance interventions are administered. In the introduction, the authors explicitly state that they decided to place the interventions before collaborative recall (i.e., before misinformation exposure), but the Method section places them after collaborative recall and after a second filler task. This is not a minor editorial inconsistency: intervention timing is central to the theoretical rationale (pre-exposure inoculation vs post-exposure warning), determines what mechanisms can operate, and directly affects interpretation and comparability with prior warning studies.
issues.quote:
What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase (that is, before exposing participants to misinformation). ...

After that, the third phase will take place: it will consist in the procedures to reduce vulnerability to misinformation that were described above.

issues.subcategory: memory test format contradiction
issues.description: The manuscript describes the final individual memory test as open-ended in the Methods section, with four indices derived from open-ended responses, but the Analysis Plan then states that the individual memory test will also use a two-alternative forced-choice format. These formats produce qualitatively different response processes, different susceptibility estimates, and different scoring rules. Because the planned analyses and construct being measured depend on test format, this inconsistency prevents evaluation of the actual design.
issues.quote:
Immediately after the participants are done with the methods of reducing memory conformity (or the control condition), they will complete the individual memory test... The test will contain 20 open-ended questions... Four indices will be derived from the open-ended test...

In the present research, the individual memory test will also use the two-alternative forced-choice format.

issues.subcategory: mismatch in intervention timing rationale vs prior literature summary
issues.description: The authors first state, regarding the present study, that they decided to place the warning after collaborative recall, but later state they decided to place the methods before collaborative recall. These are directly incompatible descriptions of the same study. Since the timing of warning is a major manipulated feature in misinformation research, this contradiction undermines confidence in the protocol and in the validity of the stated hypotheses.
issues.quote:
In the present study we decided to place the warning after the collaborative recall (see the rationale for the research below).

What is important, we decided to place the methods inducing resistance to misinformation before the collaborative recall phase (that is, before exposing participants to misinformation).

issues.subcategory: unit-of-analysis/dependence from dyadic design not addressed
issues.description: Participants are tested in pairs, jointly watch and discuss materials, and pairs are randomly assigned to condition. This creates non-independence of observations within dyads. However, the analysis plan treats the data as if all 240 participants are independent in a repeated-measures ANOVA, and the power analysis also uses participant counts without accounting for clustering. Ignoring dyadic dependence can inflate Type I error, misestimate standard errors, and overstate effective sample size. The appropriate unit may be the individual with dyad-level clustering, or the dyad for some outcomes, but this is not addressed.
issues.quote: The sample size will be set at 240 people (120 pairs)... Pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups... The results will be analyzed by means of a two-factor ANOVA

issues.subcategory: power analysis ignores clustering by pair
issues.description: The power analysis assumes 240 participants, but assignment is by pair and the main social manipulation occurs within pairs. Effective sample size is therefore lower than 240 if pair members' outcomes are correlated. Because the power calculation does not incorporate intraclass correlation or dyadic nesting, the study may be substantially underpowered for the interaction effects that are the main target.
issues.quote: The sample size will be set at 240 people (120 pairs)... Pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups... Considering the accessible financial, organizational and time resources, a sample of 240 participants was assumed

issues.subcategory: improper effect-size synthesis for repeated-measures ANOVA planning
issues.description: The manuscript derives a repeated-measures ANOVA effect size (Cohen's f) from a meta-analytic Hedges' g pooled across two studies. It is unclear whether the original g values were comparable, whether they represented within-subject standardized mean differences, and how the conversion to f was performed. This is especially problematic because one source effect is extremely large (g = 1.92) and the pooled estimate comes from only two heterogeneous studies. The resulting sample-size estimate of 18 for the conformity effect is likely unstable and not informative for the actual mixed design.
issues.quote:
The existing results as regards effect sizes are Hedges’ g = 1.92, N = 55 (Ito et al., 2019) and Hedges’ g = 0.38, N = 74 (Kękuś et al., 2020).

Given the rather large difference in effect sizes between both studies, random effects were assumed while calculating the joint effect size, which was 1.13. This amounts to a Cohen f of about 0.57.

issues.subcategory: unsupported pooled correlation estimate
issues.description: The authors use a repeated-measures correlation of r = 0.07 as an input for power analysis based on 'both studies available,' but provide no derivation details and the value is implausibly low for within-person accuracy across item types from the same test. Because repeated-measures ANOVA power is sensitive to this parameter, a poorly justified correlation undermines the sample-size calculation.
issues.quote: The joint correlation of results in the discussed and non-discussed items in both studies available was 0.07... A correlation r = 0.07 between repeated measures was assumed based on the research described above

issues.subcategory: directional tests in ANOVA power analysis not justified
issues.description: The power analysis states that 'directional significance tests are assumed' for planned comparisons. In the context of ANOVA interactions and multiple pairwise group comparisons, one-tailed testing is unusual and requires strong preregistered directional hypotheses for each comparison. Using directional tests can artificially reduce required sample size. The manuscript does not justify this choice or specify for which comparisons one-tailed tests would be used.
issues.quote: Comparisons among all groups and directional significance tests are assumed.

issues.subcategory: unclear primary outcome among multiple indices
issues.description: The authors propose analyzing four indices from the final test (correct answers, misinformation-consistent answers, other answers, overall number of answers), and also 'average accuracy on the filler, non-discussed, and discussed questions.' No single primary endpoint is specified, nor is any multiplicity correction or hierarchical testing plan provided. This leaves substantial researcher degrees of freedom in selecting favorable outcomes after seeing the data.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test’s scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers. Moreover, we will observe the individual memory test’s average accuracy on the filler, non-discussed, and discussed questions.

issues.subcategory: ambiguous scoring rules for misinformation exposure
issues.description: The scoring plan changes definition midstream. One paragraph says discussed items will be scored based on whether the partner actually provided misleading information; another says all discussed items will be categorized as containing misinformation because the procedure is designed to expose participants to differing versions. These are materially different coding schemes. Treating all discussed items as misinformation regardless of what was actually said can misclassify exposure and dilute or distort the conformity effect. The unresolved ambiguity introduces analytic flexibility and threatens validity.
issues.quote:
In this case, each answer given by the partner of a participant that is inconsistent with what the participant was presented with is misleading... However, if the partner provided an answer consistent with what the participant had seen... the situation will not be classified as misleading.

In addition, while scoring the individual memory test accuracy on the discussed questions (items containing misleading information), we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner’s differing version of events.

issues.subcategory: operationalization of misinformation exposure does not match actual exposure
issues.description: The plan to classify all discussed critical items as misinformation-containing because the procedure was designed that way does not validly operationalize actual misinformation exposure. In social discussion paradigms, some pairs may fail to mention the critical discrepant detail, may guess the participant's own version, or may not reach agreement. Conformity should be analyzed conditional on actual receipt of discrepant information, not presumed receipt. Otherwise the measure conflates discussion opportunity with misinformation exposure.
issues.quote: we will categorize all discussed items as having contained misinformation, as the collaborative recall procedure is designed to expose participants to their partner’s differing version of events.

issues.subcategory: discussion content not standardized while exposure presumed
issues.description: Although the discussion is audio recorded, the authors do not indicate that discussion transcripts will be coded to verify whether misinformation was actually mentioned, how strongly it was asserted, whether participants agreed, or whether one partner dominated. Since the social manipulation is delivered through unstructured discussion, without coding the manipulation fidelity is unknown. This is especially important because the intervention efficacy depends on how much misinformation participants actually encounter.
issues.quote: If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented. The discussion will be audio recorded.

issues.subcategory: randomization procedure insufficiently specified
issues.description: The manuscript says pairs will be randomly assigned to four groups but provides no details on the randomization method, allocation concealment, blocking, or balancing across participant characteristics. Given the dyadic design and age restrictions, these details are necessary to assess selection bias and reproducibility.
issues.quote: Pairs of participants will be randomly assigned to one of four groups

issues.subcategory: blinding not described
issues.description: There is no discussion of whether experimenters administering conditions, coding open-ended responses, or transcribing discussions will be blind to condition and hypotheses. Because outcomes include open-ended scoring and potentially subjective coding of misinformation-consistent responses, lack of blinding can introduce bias. Replication and validity require explicit reporting of who was blinded and how.
issues.quote: Four indices will be derived from the open-ended test: the number of: (1) correct answers... (2) answers consistent with the misinformation...

issues.subcategory: intervention duration and modality not matched across groups
issues.description: The interventions differ not only in content but likely in task demands, engagement, and modality. Two conditions involve ~7-minute podcasts, while the Demonstration and motivation condition adds an interactive DRM task plus feedback and then a motivational podcast/instruction. The control receives a podcast only. Any differences could reflect extra time, cognitive activation, self-generated retrieval, arousal, or demand rather than the theorized mechanisms. Without an active, time- and engagement-matched control, causal interpretation of condition differences is weakened.
issues.quote: The extended warning will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast... The training will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast... First, in order to demonstrate... a substantially shortened and simplified procedure based on the DRM paradigm will be used... Next, the participants’ motivation... will consist in them listening to a podcast... In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.

issues.subcategory: demonstration manipulation may induce general memory distrust rather than resistance to misinformation
issues.description: The DRM-based demonstration is intended to show vulnerability to influence, but DRM false recall primarily indexes associative false memory under semantic activation, not co-witness misinformation specifically. The manipulation may therefore induce generalized distrust in one's memory rather than improved source monitoring or resistance to social misinformation. The authors note this possibility but still interpret the condition as targeting suggestive influence. This construct mismatch complicates interpretation of null or positive effects.
issues.quote: The demonstration of the fallibility of memory will be done by means of the DRM technique... Demonstrating the individual fallibility of memory should make the participants alert to the real possibility that their reports may be distorted as a result of a discussion with the partner.

issues.subcategory: education intervention lacks direct measure of proposed mechanism
issues.description: The Education about memory condition is hypothesized to affect metamemory, source monitoring, and perhaps memory efficacy, but no direct measures of these constructs are included. Without manipulation checks or mediator measures, the authors cannot assess whether the intervention actually changed the targeted mechanisms or whether any observed effects occurred through alternative pathways.
issues.quote: We assume that the lecture will also enhance memory monitoring, sense of memory efficacy or even memory-related affect.

issues.subcategory: confidence ratings collected but not integrated into hypotheses/analysis
issues.description: Participants will rate certainty for each answer, yet the analysis plan never explains how confidence will be analyzed despite confidence being central to the theoretical rationale (e.g., reliance on own memory vs partner due to confidence). This is a missed opportunity and also a construct-validity problem because one of the proposed mechanisms explicitly concerns confidence and trust in memory.
issues.quote:
for each question, the participants will be asked to rate the subjective certainty of each answer on a scale from 0%... to 100%...

Finally, we assumed that telling the participants that many people give wrong answers because of the lack of confidence in their own correct memories would make the participants more prone to rely on their own memories.

issues.subcategory: claims about ruling out normative influence are overstated
issues.description: The authors assert that normative influence is 'completely ruled out' because the final test is individual. This is conceptually incorrect. Social conformity effects can persist into later private judgments due to internalization, anticipated evaluation, relationship concerns, or residual social pressures from the prior interaction. Ruling out normative influence would require stronger design features and direct measures, not merely a private test. This overstatement narrows interpretation inappropriately.
issues.quote: Given the fact that the individual memory test does not include any element of direct interpersonal pressure, we assumed that the normative impact explanation of the memory conformity effect is completely ruled out in this study

issues.subcategory: misapplication of inoculation framework given actual intervention timing
issues.description: The Demonstration and motivation condition is framed as inoculation against future influence, and the manuscript argues that interventions are placed before misinformation exposure. But the actual procedure places the interventions after collaborative recall, i.e., after social misinformation has already occurred. Inoculation theory concerns pre-exposure resistance. If the intervention is post-exposure, the theoretical framing is mismatched and the hypothesized mechanism changes from prevention to correction.
issues.quote:
The main reason for that is that we wanted to inoculate participants against the influence of misinformation before it could take effect.

After that, the third phase will take place: it will consist in the procedures to reduce vulnerability to misinformation

issues.subcategory: counterbalancing claim conflicts with fixed discussed items
issues.description: The design section states that discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced, but the procedure later says all pairs will discuss the same set of four critical details 'in order to ensure sufficient discussion.' These statements cannot both be true. Fixing the same items as discussed for everyone confounds discussion status with item content/difficulty and undermines the within-subject comparison.
issues.quote:
In the study, the memory conformity effect will be measured in a within-subjects design and discussed and non-discussed items will be fully counterbalanced.

In order to ensure sufficient discussion, each pair will discuss the same set of four critical details during the collaborative recall phase.

issues.subcategory: number of critical-discussion items ambiguous
issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently describes the collaborative recognition test as including four critical details among 12 questions, while the final test includes eight critical details regardless of whether they were discussed. This is plausible if four are discussed and four non-discussed, but the text elsewhere suggests counterbalancing and all discussed items being treated as misinformation-containing. The exact mapping of the eight critical details across discussed/non-discussed conditions is not clearly specified, limiting replicability.
issues.quote:
The test will comprise 12 questions, four of which refer to critical details... 

The test will contain 20 open-ended questions, eight of which will cover all the critical details included in the movie, regardless of whether they were subsequently discussed.

issues.subcategory: insufficient detail on collaborative recall procedure and coding
issues.description: Important procedural details are missing: whether participants respond orally or jointly select options, how disagreement is handled analytically, whether each partner's statements are transcribed verbatim, how 'both responses will be documented,' and how exposure strength will be coded. These are necessary to evaluate manipulation fidelity and reproduce the study.
issues.quote: Each question and its five possible responses will be displayed in a PowerPoint presentation for 60 seconds while participants discuss the answer. If the participants are unable to reach an agreement, both responses will be documented. The discussion will be audio recorded.

issues.subcategory: no scoring protocol for open-ended responses
issues.description: If the final test is open-ended, the manuscript does not explain how responses will be coded as correct, misinformation-consistent, or other; how ambiguous answers, synonyms, partial answers, multiple answers, or omissions will be handled; whether coding will be done independently by multiple raters; or how inter-rater reliability will be assessed. Without this information, the primary outcome is not reproducible.
issues.quote: Four indices will be derived from the open-ended test: the number of: (1) correct answers... (2) answers consistent with the misinformation, (3) other answers...

issues.subcategory: missing data handling absent
issues.description: The manuscript gives no plan for handling missing responses on the final test, missing confidence ratings, incomplete DRM worksheets, or missing discussion data. The only exclusion criterion is technical problems. In repeated-measures and item-level designs, missing data decisions can materially affect results; these should be prespecified.
issues.quote:
3.1. Exclusions

We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.

issues.subcategory: no plan for participant exclusions beyond technical failures
issues.description: There is no prespecified handling of participants who discover the MORI manipulation, fail to comply with instructions (e.g., peeking around glasses), do not engage in discussion, are non-native speakers, provide no answers, or show extreme suspicion. Because these factors can strongly affect misinformation susceptibility, omission of exclusion rules creates analytic flexibility and threatens validity.
issues.quote:
We will exclude participants in the case of any technical problems during the experimental session.

Next, the subjects will be requested to say what they think the real purpose of the study was. Their responses will be recorded for exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance.

issues.subcategory: hypothesis awareness assessed but not prespecified for exclusion or adjustment
issues.description: The authors collect suspicion/hypothesis-awareness data but state it will only be recorded for exploratory analysis. They do not prespecify whether participants who identify the deception or purpose will be excluded, analyzed separately, or included unchanged. This leaves flexibility that can materially influence observed effects in deception-based paradigms.
issues.quote: Next, the subjects will be requested to say what they think the real purpose of the study was. Their responses will be recorded for exploratory analysis of any relationship between hypothesis awareness and performance.

issues.subcategory: age-based confounding within pairs not actually controlled
issues.description: The authors restrict the age range to 16–35 to avoid very young participants discussing with elderly ones, but this does not address substantial within-pair age differences within that range, nor other dyadic characteristics known to influence conformity (e.g., familiarity, trust, relationship status, gender composition). No matching or measurement of these factors is described. Because social influence is dyadic, these are plausible confounds.
issues.quote: The age of the participants will be restricted in order to avoid a situation in which a very young participant would discuss the original material with an elderly one, which would possibly activate some confounding factors

issues.subcategory: sample limitations underacknowledged
issues.description: The sample consists of volunteers aged 16–35 recruited via media and internet advertisements, yet the discussion emphasizes implications for eyewitnesses and justice systems generally. Young volunteer community samples in laboratory dyads may not generalize to actual witnesses, older adults, children, high-stress crimes, or legally consequential testimony. These limits are not meaningfully acknowledged in the design rationale.
issues.quote:
The participants enrolled in the study will be 16–35 years old; they will be invited to participate via advertisements in the media and on the internet.

The main reason for its popularity is the fact that the MORI technique brings laboratory conditions closer to the real-life situations in which witnesses discuss a crime and are then individually interviewed by law enforcement officers.

issues.subcategory: ecological validity overclaim for MORI paradigm
issues.description: The manuscript describes the MORI technique as bringing laboratory conditions closer to real-life witness situations, but the actual event is a short silent video, misinformation is limited to a few visual details, and testimony occurs immediately in a low-stakes lab setting. The interventions are also artificial podcasts/DRM tasks. The leap from this setup to justice-system functioning is too strong without qualification.
issues.quote: The main reason for its popularity is the fact that the MORI technique brings laboratory conditions closer to the real-life situations in which witnesses discuss a crime and are then individually interviewed by law enforcement officers.

issues.subcategory: mechanistic predictions not clearly differentiated across interventions
issues.description: The three interventions overlap substantially in content (memory fallibility, source issues, motivation to rely on own memory), and the manuscript itself acknowledges this overlap. Yet it also predicts an effectiveness ordering across interventions based on different mechanisms. Without sharper theoretical differentiation and manipulation checks, any differences or null differences will be hard to interpret.
issues.quote: Secondly, we are aware of some overlap between the three interventions, for instance, teaching about memory is included is present in a way in both Education about memory and Demonstration and motivation.

issues.subcategory: exploratory analyses not bounded
issues.description: The manuscript includes an exploratory analysis using DRM performance as a predictor of MORI results, but does not define the outcome, model, covariates, or whether this will be individual- or dyad-level. Combined with multiple possible final-test indices, this adds substantial analytical freedom.
issues.quote: As an additional exploratory analysis, the results on the DRM procedure will be used as a possible predictor of the results on the MORI technique.

issues.subcategory: ANOVA on bounded count outcomes may violate model assumptions
issues.description: The primary outcomes are small counts of correct, misinformation-consistent, and other answers across a limited number of critical items (e.g., 0–4 or 0–8), which are bounded and likely non-normal. A standard ANOVA may be inappropriate, especially with repeated measures and dyadic clustering. Generalized mixed models at the item level would better respect the data structure and exposure variation.
issues.quote: We will explore the individual memory test’s scores for the critical details using analysis of variance (ANOVA), using all four indices: the number of correct answers, number of answers consistent with misinformation, other answers, and the overall number of answers.

issues.subcategory: possible contamination from administering interventions jointly within pair
issues.description: The procedure implies that both members of a pair undergo the same intervention together after their discussion. Especially in the DRM and motivational conditions, joint administration may create further social influence, discussion, or mutual interpretation beyond the intended manipulation. No steps are described to prevent post-discussion interaction during the interventions, which could itself affect conformity or source monitoring.
issues.quote: The participants will be randomly divided into four groups... At this moment in this group, the experimenter will give the following information to the participants... Afterwards, the participants will be motivated...

issues.subcategory: materials not sufficiently specified for replication
issues.description: The exact scripts/transcripts for the podcasts, DRM word lists, control podcast content, and collaborative recognition questions are not provided. Given that the interventions are novel and content-sensitive, replication and interpretation require the full wording or at least enough detail to reconstruct them precisely.
issues.quote: The extended warning will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast... The training will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast... Four lists will be chosen which on the basis of our previous research with this procedure, produce the strongest effect.

issues.subcategory: selection of strongest DRM lists introduces undisclosed flexibility
issues.description: The DRM manipulation will use four lists chosen because, based on prior research, they 'produce the strongest effect.' However, the source data, selection criteria, and exact lists are not fully justified or preregistered. Choosing the strongest lists can maximize apparent manipulation success and may not generalize; more importantly, the exact implementation must be fixed in advance for a confirmatory design.
issues.quote: Four lists will be chosen which on the basis of our previous research with this procedure, produce the strongest effect.

issues.subcategory: intervention effects confounded with deception revelation/enlightenment
issues.description: The Extended warning includes 'an enlightenment regarding the purpose of the deception' and informs participants the partner may have seen a different version. If this occurs after collaborative recall, it changes not just caution but participants' understanding of the entire procedure. Any reduction in conformity could result from revealing the manipulation rather than from the theorized warning components. The intervention bundles multiple causal ingredients without means to separate them.
issues.quote:
- an enlightenment regarding the purpose of the deception.

Extended warning, informing that the partner actually saw a different version of the movie and informing why the deception was applied, should make the participants who are aware of discrepancies discard the consistency assumption

issues.subcategory: control podcast may not be psychologically inert
issues.description: The control condition uses a podcast about 'soft skills related to social attitudes,' but there is no justification that this topic is neutral with respect to social influence, conformity, motivation, or metacognition. If the control content affects interpersonal attitudes or vigilance, it may bias estimates of intervention efficacy.
issues.quote: In the control group, participants will listen to a podcast concerning soft skills related to social attitudes.

issues.subcategory: no manipulation checks for intervention uptake
issues.description: There are no measures to verify whether participants understood or remembered the podcasts, accepted the warning, believed the DRM feedback, or felt motivated to rely on their own memory. Without manipulation checks, null effects are uninterpretable because the interventions may simply have failed to engage participants.
issues.quote: The extended warning will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast... The training will take the form of an approximately 7-minute podcast... The motivational aspect will be achieved by a podcast
